newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises as Europeans bicker over currency rates.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises as Europeans bicker over currency rates.

text.p: The dollar rallied against major European currencies Friday as European leaders reiterated their desire for a stronger U.S. currency and interest rates tumbled in Europe's bond markets.
French policy makers continued to press their German counterparts to allow the dollar to rise against the French franc and German mark, without apparent success.
Bank of France Gov. Jean-Claude Trichet said he saw no reason to devalue the franc against the mark, but failed to rule out a dollar rally against European currencies.

Traders read that as tacit approval of Bank of France monetary council member Jean-Pierre Gerard's statement Thursday that Germany and France should lower official interest rates to push the dollar higher.

Lower interest rates abroad make dollar-denominated assets more attractive, boosting the dollar's value. A stronger dollar also would make French and German exports more competitive in the United States.

"Today's market has been very much a dollar/Europe play, with dollar gains across the board as the French and German currency debate goes on," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.
German leaders have said little during the latest flurry of French comments, suggesting grudging agreement with the French position, dealers said.
Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick was quoted as welcoming the dollar's recent gains vs. the mark as a boon to German exporters.
French officials have sought to boost the dollar to ease the transition to a single European currency planned for 1999.

"In a sense, France is holding a loaded gun to Germany's head saying either we revalue the mark (vs. the franc) or Europe as a bloc devalues against the U.S. and the rest of the world," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
The dollar rose to 1.5386 marks from 1.5320 at Thursday's European close and to 113.84 Japanese yen from 113.62.
The dollar also rose to 1.3040 Swiss francs from 1.2958 and to 5.2255 French francs from 5.2006.
In other trading, the British pound rose to $1.6825 from $1.6772. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3503 from C$1.3461.
Trading was closed in the United States Thursday in observance of the Thanksgiving Day holiday.

European bond markets rallied Friday, led by German bunds which posted record highs. The ensuing drop in interest rates, which move in the opposite direction from bond prices, fuelled dollar buying, dealers said.
That put particular pressure on the Swiss franc, as low Swiss interest rates have encouraged many investors to sell francs to invest in bonds elsewhere.

"(The Swiss) need the currency weaker to stimulate their economy," said David Ethridge, director of currency analysis in North America at MMS International. "Unless there's some surprising news, people are going to remain short Swiss."
